headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: xonsh can read/write broad filesystem and egress network, while awesome-prompts is a prompt repository that may be treated as trusted input.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no I/O surfaces and is not runnable, so it cannot directly inject B. But B reads filesystem contents and can execute shell/Python, so if A's prompt files are copied into B's workspace, B may treat attacker-controlled text as instructions. The pathway is plausible but not default and depends on shared files, so medium fits.
conditions: IF A's prompt content is placed in a filesystem path that B reads
IF B parses that content as instructions rather than inert text
mitigations: Store A's prompts in a read-only directory
Require B to open prompt files in a plain-text viewer first
Add a manual review step before B executes any copied prompt
Use separate workspaces for prompt libraries and execution
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to files before B consumes them

B_data_leakage.rationale: B has broad filesystem read/write and network egress, so it can exfiltrate any sensitive files it can access. A touches no data classes and has no egress, so the main leakage path is from shared files into B's outbound network. Because the shared-workspace assumption is not explicit, this is an inferred but credible medium risk.
conditions: IF A's outputs or nearby files contain sensitive data
IF B can read those files from its workspace
IF B sends file contents over the network
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of B's workspace
Disable network access for B during review runs
Use a separate non-sensitive staging directory
Review B's outbound destinations before execution
requires-engineering: enforce per-directory network egress controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or network capabilities and is not runnable, while B can write the filesystem but cannot modify git state and supports only one instance. There is no documented overlapping mutable resource beyond generic filesystem access, so conflict is limited and requires unusual setup. The pair is not strongly conflicting by default.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
IF A's prompt artifacts are edited manually while B writes files there
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Make A's repository read-only
Run B in a scratch workspace
Avoid concurrent edits to the same path
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared outputs

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a prompt repository, so its outputs can become instructions or templates that B may execute or operationalize. B has shell and subprocess execution, so if it trusts A's content without verification, mistakes can cascade into incorrect commands or file changes. This is a plausible default workflow risk, but not enough for high because no direct action chain is documented.
conditions: IF B uses A's prompt text as authoritative operational guidance
IF B executes commands derived from that text without verification
mitigations: Require B to summarize before acting
Add a human approval step for generated commands
Cross-check A's output against a second source
Limit B to dry-run mode first
requires-engineering: add policy checks before command execution

E_compliance.rationale: No compliance-sensitive data class, residency mismatch, or retention policy is documented for either agent. A touches no data classes and B's listed data classes are operational artifacts rather than regulated personal data, so no compliance breach pathway is evidenced.
conditions: IF either agent is later configured to process regulated personal data
IF a separate deployment policy imposes residency or retention constraints
mitigations: Document data-class boundaries
Keep regulated data out of both agents
Review retention settings before deployment
